newsitem.title: GABON: Gabon premier, ruling party win parliament seats.
newsitem.headline: Gabon premier, ruling party win parliament seats.

text.p: Gabon's prime minister and a handful of members of his government were among early winners from the Central African nation's confused weekend parliamentary election, unofficial results showed on Monday.

The National Electoral Commission, which organised Sunday's poll, declined all comment on the results, which were published in the government newspaper L'Union and showed President Omar Bongo's Gabonese Democratic Party winning 14 seats.
There was no immediate word on how the opposition had fared in the poll, part of a 1994 deal to defuse political unrest stemming from Bongo's disputed re-election a year earlier.
More than 1,000 candidates were bidding for 120 seats in the national assembly. Gabon, an oil-producing former French colony of 1.2 million people, has an electorate of 550,000.

Lengthy delays in the distribution of voting materials disrupted the repeatedly delayed elections. Witnesses said confusion over electoral lists, which were posted late and missed names, further complicated polling.
"Everything has to start somewhere," Bongo said after casting his vote, adding things would get better with time.

Voters in Libreville, some of whom had queued from dawn, remained calm, with no reports of major incident. Reports from elsewhere said voting stations or materials were ransacked in three southern towns with unspecified incidents in two others.
Early winners, according to L'Union, included Prime Minister Paulin Obame-Nguema, Bongo's son and advisor Ali and the ministers of oil, transport, agriculture and construction.
Past experience suggests results could take over a week to trickle out. A second round is scheduled for December 29.
Bongo has ruled Gabon since 1968 after the death of Gabon's founding head of state, Leon Mba.
His party was expected to face strong competition from the National Woodcutters Rally, led by Father Paul Mba Abessole, a Roman Catholic priest and runner-up in 1993.
Sunday's vote was Gabon's second multiparty legislative polls. The first were in 1990 when a wave of democratic reform swept across Africa after the fall of Soviet-bloc communism.
Government and opposition agreed the 1994 Paris Accords after political unrest killed over a dozen people.
